comparedAgainst: https://codeblog.jonskeet.uk/category/edulinq/ (Jon Skeet's 'Reimplementing LINQ to Objects' / Edulinq series, which builds Where and Select from scratch with yield return)
justification: Strong, genuinely differentiated coverage of a commonly-covered topic, with one real factual overreach that a careful technical reader will catch. Originality: the two closest precedents for 'build your own LINQ operator' are Jon Skeet's Edulinq series (Where/Select via iterator blocks, no traced side-by-side comparison against the real operators, no re-enumeration-cost measurement, no IQueryable proof) and Microsoft's own 'Deferred execution example' page (a single ConvertCollectionToUpperCase extension method with Console.WriteLine tracing — the tracing-print technique itself is a known pedagogical device, but this article's combination is not: a help-desk-ticket domain, three chained custom operators (Traced/MyWhere/MySelect) whose pull-based interleaving is diagrammed, then run byte-for-byte alongside the real Where/Select on the same data and predicate to prove equivalence, then extended with a MyTakeWhile exercise that proves early-termination streaming). No sentence-level matches to either source were found on spot-check. The IQueryable section's proof — walking a quoted LambdaExpression's Unquote/BinaryExpression/MemberExpression/ConstantExpression to read a field name and comparison value out of the tree without ever calling the predicate — is a distinctive, original construction; most competing material stops at printing `query.Expression.ToString()`. Sourcing: all 7 Microsoft Learn URLs in front matter resolve and are accurately represented — I fetched all seven directly. Every direct quotation ('stores all the information that is required to perform the action', 'Calling an iterator doesn't execute it immediately', 'is supported directly in the C# language by the yield keyword', 'at the point in the code where the query is declared' / 'when the query variable is enumerated' / 'the results might differ every time', 'generates a MethodCallExpression', 'causes the expression tree ... to be executed' / 'specific to a query provider' / 'may involve translating the expression tree...') is verbatim-accurate and used in the context the source supports. The task brief asked me to verify a specific claim about an old 'classification of standard query operators' URL 404ing and being folded into 'Introduction to LINQ Queries' — the article does not actually assert any such 404/redirect history anywhere in its text; it simply cites 'Introduction to LINQ Queries' for the immediate/deferred/streaming/nonstreaming classification, and I confirmed by fetching that page directly that this classification (including the 'Classification of standard query operators by manner of execution' heading and table) is a live, current section of that exact page today — so the citation is accurate and there is no invented redirect story to flag. All 7 sources are cited inline at the point of the claim (none are name-only or uncited), satisfying the binding 'cite where the claim is made' rule. No filler: the opening sentence states the bug directly, there is no restated-title intro, no 'In this article', no boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion headings, and the piece ends inside the third exercise's solution rather than a summary paragraph. No ad code or ad placeholders. Toolchain statement ('.NET 10.0.12, Windows 11, x64, on a desktop Core i7-11700K') appears exactly once, in its own sentence, immediately beside the re-enumeration-cost measurement in 'What re-enumerating costs' — not as an opening provenance stamp, matching the binding rule. Structure variety: the only sibling currently in the pillar is value-types-vs-reference-types.md (garbage-collection.md and async-await.md are not yet written); headings in both are specific to content ('The SLA count that didn't add up', 'What yield return actually builds' vs. 'One assignment, two outcomes', 'Boxing: a value gets an object of its own') with no shared template, and both place a mid-article exercise plus a closing 'Practice:'-style section rather than a generic 'Exercises' heading — an organizational similarity but not a copy-paste template (heading text, exercise count and forms all differ). Exercise variety and no leaking: 'Predict the trace order' (predict-the-output form) correctly withholds its output block until inside :::solution; 'Find the bug: two lookups became eight' shows its output before the solution, but that is the intended shape for a find-the-bug exercise (the wrong number is the puzzle, not the answer) and matches the brief's guidance to vary exercise form rather than banning output display outright; 'Extend it: a streaming operator that stops early' is a build-it exercise entirely inside the solution. All three forms differ from each other and from the mid-article exercise, satisfying the anti-template rule. Phone-width: max code-line length is exactly 60 characters (at the limit, not over) and max output-line length is 32 characters, both inside the stated budget and in the same range as the sibling article's own measured 59/40. run-code.mjs: PASS, blocks=22, executed=11, matching the expected counts. The one real defect, and the reason this isn't higher: 'Writing Where and Select from scratch' closes with 'The real Enumerable.Where and Enumerable.Select are more careful about edge cases ... but they are, at heart, the same foreach loop with a yield return guarded by an if.' I fetched the actual dotnet/runtime source for Where.cs directly (the file the article's own citation links to): the primary Where(IEnumerable<TSource>, Func<TSource,bool>) overload does not use yield return at all — it dispatches to hand-written iterator classes (IEnumerableWhereIterator, ArrayWhereIterator, ListWhereIterator) each with an explicit MoveNext() containing a while/if loop; the only yield return in the file is in the separate indexed-overload's WhereIterator method. The article's own printed diagnostic a few lines earlier in the same section ('SizeOptIListWhereIterator`1') is itself evidence of a hand-rolled iterator class, not a compiler-generated yield state machine, so the claim is contradicted by the article's own captured output as well as by the primary source. This is an unsupported/incorrect technical claim of exactly the kind the brief's 'generalisations get checked' lesson warns about, and it undercuts the 'mine vs. real' payoff the section is building toward. It is cheap to fix (state the conceptual equivalence — same guard, same one-item-at-a-time pull — without claiming the real implementation literally uses yield return) and does not affect run-code correctness or any other section. With that one claim corrected this article would be at or above 9.0; as written it clears the 8.5 bar comfortably but is held back from the top of the range by a checkable factual overreach in its own closing argument.

issues.location: Section 'Writing `Where` and `Select` from scratch', closing paragraph after the `id=compare` code/output block: "The real `Enumerable.Where` and `Enumerable.Select` are more careful about edge cases (null checks, an indexed overload, a fast path when the source is an array or a `List<T>`) but they are, at heart, the same `foreach` loop with a `yield return` guarded by an `if`."
issues.problem: Verified directly against the dotnet/runtime source for Where.cs (the file linked from the article's own Enumerable.Where citation): the primary Where(IEnumerable<TSource>, Func<TSource,bool>) overload does not use `yield return` anywhere. It dispatches to hand-written iterator classes (IEnumerableWhereIterator<TSource>, ArrayWhereIterator<TSource>, ListWhereIterator<TSource>), each implementing MoveNext() directly as a while-loop with an if-guarded return, for allocation/dispatch performance. The only `yield return` in the whole file is in the separate WhereIterator method that backs the indexed overload. The article's own printed output two code blocks earlier in this same section ('SizeOptIListWhereIterator`1') is itself the name of one of these hand-written classes, not a compiler-generated <Where>d__N state machine that `yield return` would produce — so the claim is contradicted by the article's own captured evidence, not just by the external source.
issues.fixLooksLike: Replace the 'at heart, the same foreach loop with a yield return guarded by an if' claim with an accurate conceptual statement, e.g.: 'they are conceptually the same — one predicate check per source element, one item pulled at a time — but the production implementation (the SizeOptIListWhereIterator printed above) is a hand-written class with its own MoveNext, not a compiler-generated yield state machine; .NET avoids the state-machine allocation for these hot-path operators.' Cite or simply describe what was verified rather than asserting the internal mechanism is literally the same as the article's own MyWhere/MySelect.
